Read this before writing anything

The site already has 76 pages. They were read from the live sitemaps, not guessed. Rows marked Live already exist — do not rewrite them; their only job now is to receive links from the new articles. Rows marked Overlaps have a live page covering part of the topic; write the new page only if it says something the live one does not, and link the two. Rows marked Write are genuinely missing.

The blog currently holds one post. Almost the entire supporting layer below is greenfield, which is why the plan is weighted toward long-tail articles that feed the service and industry pages that already exist.

CornerstoneThe pages the whole site points at. 4,000–6,000 words, permanently maintained, at the site root.
PillarThe hub of one topic cluster. 2,500–3,500 words. Links down to everything in its cluster, up to its cornerstone.
Sub-hubOne industry, workflow, city or market. 2,000–2,800 words. Usually a /industries/ or /services/ page.
SupportingThe long tail, in /blog/. 1,400–2,200 words on one specific question. Fast to rank, and it feeds its sub-hub.

      House rules

      1. Never republish a Live row. It exists. Open it, add the inbound links listed under it, and move on.
      2. Ship whole clusters. Pick a cluster, write its pillar, then its sub-hubs, then the supporting pages. A finished cluster of twelve beats eighty scattered posts.
      3. Place every link on publish day. Each row lists its links: one up to the parent, three across to siblings, one to the money page, and for hubs, one down to each child. Retrofitting links across 1,200 pages is a project nobody ever finishes.
      4. Use the suggested anchor. The link sheet gives the target's primary keyword as anchor text. Vary the wording naturally; keep the meaning.
      5. Validate volume before the big pages. Competition ratings come from a real 126-competitor analysis. Search volume does not — check the keyword in Google Keyword Planner (location = United Arab Emirates) before committing to a cornerstone.
      6. Arabic is written, never translated. The English gloss under each Arabic title is for navigating this page only. It must never appear on the published article.
      7. One real thing per page — a screenshot, an AED figure, a named integration, a genuine client outcome. Never invented. That is both the ranking edge and the legal safety.
